Annan is one of six co-chairs at this year's WEF gathering, along with news tycoon Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Werner Wenning of the German chemical group Bayer, Indian industrialist Anand G. He also urged delegates to address three interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy and security, and climate change. "It is important leaders work on ways of finding effective, far-reaching policies -- even if they are radical -- that will allow us to create sustainable economic growth and create jobs for those who are out of jobs," Annan said. Newscorp. CEO Murdoch said delegates needed to be "absolutely honest about where the world is at this point," warning that the consequences of $50 trillion being wiped off personal fortunes had left people feeling "depressed and traumatized." "We've been living in the Western world way above our means. We've been on a great binge and it's come to an end and we have to live though the correction," Murdoch said. But he said the downturn offered a chance to set about tackling issues of energy sufficiency and pollution. "We must treat this crisis, whether it lasts for a year or five years, as an opportunity to set goals for how we want to come out of it. This is a time to shape the policies to help to solve some of those problems." HSBC boss Green said the banking industry needed to admit that it had not "covered itself in glory" in contributing to the collapse of the financial industry and called for continuing government intervention to "stop a nasty recession spiraling down into something else." But he said the major banks could contribute to solving the crisis as well: "I do not believe for a moment that you can have a successful economy without successful and properly functioning international capital markets." Wenning said he didn't expect any solutions to emerge from this year's meeting, but hoped delegates could achieve "a joint understanding of the reasons for the financial crisis" and called for a return to "the basics of sustainable behavior." "If we are really able to address these mega-challenges of the future then we would be able to restore the trust in leadership -- and I believe the world needs leadership." Political leaders will join the discussions later Wednesday with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both due to deliver agenda-setting addresses.

# Davos Forum Opens with Calls for Radical UN Reform Amid Global Crisis

DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN) — The global economic downturn has laid bare a profound "crisis of global governance" that can only be remedied through sweeping reform of the United Nations, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan declared Wednesday as the World Economic Forum commenced in Switzerland.

"The current architecture for managing global affairs is broken and must be repaired," Annan told delegates on the opening morning of the five-day gathering of the world's foremost political and business leaders. "We have major new players emerging on the world stage, and they must be integrated and given a voice."

Addressing the composition of the U.N. Security Council—which grants permanent seats and veto power exclusively to the United States, the United Kingdom, Russia, China, and France—Annan was unequivocal: "We cannot continue to govern the world according to the outcome of a war fought sixty years ago. The choice before us is stark: destructive competition or genuine cooperation. We live in an interdependent world, and cooperation is the only path forward."

Annan serves as one of six co-chairs at this year's WEF gathering, alongside media magnate Rupert Murdoch, HSBC Chairman Stephen Green, Bayer's Werner Wenning, Indian industrialist Anand G. Mahindra, and Maria Ramos, Chief Executive of South Africa's Transnet.

He further urged delegates to confront three deeply interconnected challenges: the global recession, energy security, and climate change. "It is essential that leaders devise effective, far-reaching policies—however radical they may be—that will foster sustainable economic growth and create employment for those who have lost their jobs," Annan emphasized.

News Corp. CEO Rupert Murdoch echoed the need for candor, insisting that delegates must be "absolutely honest about where the world stands at this juncture." He cautioned that the erosion of $50 trillion in personal wealth had left individuals feeling "depressed and traumatized."

"We in the Western world have been living far beyond our means," Murdoch remarked. "We have been on a prolonged binge, and it has come to an end. Now we must weather the correction." Yet he noted that the downturn presented a valuable opportunity to address pressing issues of energy sufficiency and environmental pollution. "We must treat this crisis—whether it endures for one year or five—as an opportunity to establish clear goals for our recovery. This is the moment to shape policies that will help resolve some of these underlying problems."

HSBC's Stephen Green acknowledged that the banking industry needed to concede it had not "covered itself in glory" in contributing to the financial collapse, and he called for sustained government intervention to "prevent a severe recession from spiraling into something far worse." Nevertheless, he maintained that major banks could play a constructive role in resolving the crisis: "I do not believe for a moment that a successful economy can exist without properly functioning international capital markets."

Wenning, for his part, tempered expectations, stating he did not anticipate concrete solutions emerging from this year's meeting. Instead, he hoped delegates might reach "a shared understanding of the root causes of the financial crisis" and renew their commitment to "the fundamentals of sustainable conduct." He added, "If we can truly rise to meet these monumental challenges of the future, we will be able to restore trust in leadership—and I believe the world is in dire need of leadership."

Political leaders are set to join the discussions later Wednesday, with Chinese Premier Wen Jiabao and Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both scheduled to deliver keynote addresses setting the agenda for the forum.

# Global Leaders Call for Overhaul of International Institutions at Davos

**DAVOS, Switzerland (CNN)** — As business and political figures gathered in Switzerland for the World Economic Forum's opening day, former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan declared that the global financial meltdown had revealed deep flaws in how the world is governed—flaws he said demand sweeping changes to the United Nations.

"The system we currently use to manage international affairs simply doesn't work anymore," Annan told attendees at the five-day summit of world leaders and executives. "Emerging powers have entered the picture, and they deserve a seat at the table and a say in decisions."

Taking aim at the U.N. Security Council's structure—which grants permanent membership and veto rights exclusively to America, Britain, Russia, China, and France—Annan argued that outdated post-war arrangements can no longer dictate global affairs. "Basing world governance on who emerged victorious from a conflict six decades ago makes no sense," he said. "Our choice is between harmful rivalry or genuine partnership. Given how interconnected nations have become, collaboration is the only viable path forward."

Annan serves alongside five other co-chairs guiding this year's forum: media magnate Rupert Murdoch, HSBC's Stephen Green, Bayer executive Werner Wenning, Indian business leader Anand G. Mahindra, and Transnet CEO Maria Ramos of South Africa. Beyond U.N. reform, Annan pressed attendees to tackle three linked crises simultaneously—economic decline, energy security, and climate change. "Leaders must pursue bold, comprehensive strategies, however unconventional, to restore lasting growth and put unemployed people back to work," he emphasized.

Rupert Murdoch struck a similarly urgent tone, insisting participants confront harsh realities head-on. He noted that the vanishing of $50 trillion in personal wealth had left many people emotionally shattered. "Western societies have been spending far beyond their capacity for too long," Murdoch remarked. "That extended spree is over, and now we must endure the painful adjustment." Still, he saw silver linings—suggesting the downturn creates room to address energy shortages and environmental damage. "Regardless of whether this crisis stretches one year or five, we should use it as motivation to define what recovery should look like and craft policies that tackle these deeper issues."

HSBC's Stephen Green conceded that banks bore responsibility for the financial system's breakdown, acknowledging the industry hadn't performed admirably. He urged governments to keep intervening to prevent a serious downturn from becoming something far worse. Yet he defended banking's essential role going forward: "A thriving economy simply cannot exist without capital markets that function properly on a global scale."

Werner Wenning tempered expectations for the summit, saying he doubted concrete fixes would emerge this year. Instead, he hoped participants might reach shared clarity on what triggered the crisis and recommit to fundamentally sound economic practices. "Successfully confronting these enormous challenges ahead could help rebuild confidence in our leaders—and the world desperately needs strong leadership right now."

Later Wednesday, the conversation shifts to political leadership, with China's Premier Wen Jiabao and Russia's Prime Minister Vladimir Putin both scheduled to deliver keynote remarks setting the tone for further discussions.

# The Crisis of Global Governance: Annan's Call for Radical U.N. Reform

Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan delivered a pointed critique of international institutions, declaring that the global economic recession has exposed nothing less than a "crisis of global governance"—one that demands fundamental and far-reaching reform of the United Nations itself. In his assessment, the economic turmoil gripping the world is not merely a financial or fiscal problem, but a symptom of deeper structural failures in how the international community organizes itself to address shared challenges.

## Rethinking the Security Council

Central to Annan's critique was a direct challenge to the composition and structure of the U.N. Security Council. He argued forcefully that the world can no longer afford to be governed according to power arrangements established in the aftermath of a war fought six decades ago. The geopolitical realities of the mid-20th century, he suggested, bear little resemblance to the multipolar world of today, where new economic and political powers have emerged onto the global stage. Annan insisted that these rising players must be meaningfully integrated into the mechanisms of global governance and given genuine voice and representation—rather than remaining sidelined by an outdated institutional framework that no longer reflects current realities.

## Cooperation Over Competition

Underlying Annan's broader argument was a fundamental principle: in today's deeply interdependent world, cooperation is not simply preferable to competition—it is the only viable path forward. He warned that destructive rivalry between nations, particularly in times of economic strain, threatens to undermine the collective capacity to solve problems that respect no borders. This interconnectedness, in his view, makes unilateral or narrowly nationalistic approaches to policy increasingly obsolete and counterproductive.

## Three Interconnected Challenges

Speaking to delegates at the World Economic Forum, Annan urged global leaders to confront three challenges that he framed as deeply intertwined rather than separate crises to be tackled in isolation:

1. **The global economic recession** — requiring coordinated policy responses rather than fragmented national efforts
2. **Energy and security** — recognizing the connections between resource access and geopolitical stability
3. **Climate change** — demanding sustained, long-term commitment despite short-term economic pressures

Annan stressed that addressing these challenges effectively might well require policies that are radical in scope and ambition, breaking from conventional approaches that have proven inadequate to the scale of the problems at hand.

## Echoes from the Business World

Annan's concerns found resonance in remarks from media magnate Rupert Murdoch, who offered a stark assessment of the psychological and financial toll of the crisis. Murdoch noted that the staggering destruction of $50 trillion in personal wealth worldwide had left populations feeling "depressed and traumatized." He attributed much of this reckoning to unsustainable habits in the Western world, observing pointedly that societies had been living "way above our means" for an extended period—a pattern of excess that the current crisis has now forced into painful correction.

Together, these voices from both diplomatic and business spheres underscored a shared recognition: the current crisis represents not just an economic downturn, but a moment demanding fundamental reassessment of how the world organizes itself—both institutionally and behaviorally—to meet the challenges of an interconnected age.

# Davos: Where Global Leaders Meet Amid Swiss Peaks

Nestled in the Swiss Alps, the small resort town of Davos transforms once a year into the epicenter of global political and economic discourse. Known primarily for its ski slopes and clean mountain air, Davos becomes home to the World Economic Forum (WEF), an annual gathering that draws heads of state, business executives, and thought leaders from around the world.

The town's transformation is remarkable. For one week each January, this otherwise quiet Swiss municipality—with a permanent population of just over 11,000—hosts thousands of visitors, including heavily secured motorcades, private jets landing at nearby airports, and a media circus that rivals major international summits.

CNN, along with other major news networks, provides extensive coverage of the event, broadcasting interviews with prime ministers, CEOs, and influential figures who converge on Davos to discuss pressing global issues. Topics typically range from economic policy and climate change to technological innovation and geopolitical tensions. CNN's correspondents often set up temporary studios in the town, conducting live interviews against the backdrop of snow-capped mountains, blending the gravity of international diplomacy with the picturesque Swiss setting.

Switzerland's choice as host nation is fitting given its long-standing reputation for neutrality and diplomatic tradition. The country's stability and discretion make it an ideal venue for sensitive discussions among competing global powers, allowing Davos to serve as a unique meeting ground where dialogue can occur outside the formal structures of organizations like the United Nations.

Critics of the World Economic Forum in Davos often point to the disconnect between the luxurious setting and the pressing global issues discussed—private jets ferrying attendees while climate change tops the agenda, for instance. Nevertheless, the event continues to attract significant international attention, with CNN and other outlets treating it as a barometer for the priorities and anxieties of global elites in any given year.

Beyond the conference itself, Davos represents an interesting intersection of local Swiss culture and global influence—a small alpine community that, for one week annually, finds itself at the center of world attention, its name synonymous not just with skiing, but with the ongoing conversation about the future of global governance and economics.

# Annan Urges Sweeping UN Reforms in Davos Address, Calls for Renewed Multilateral Cooperation

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — Former United Nations Secretary-General Kofi Annan delivered a pointed call for institutional reform at the World Economic Forum on Thursday, telling an audience of world leaders, business executives, and policymakers that the international system built after World War II is struggling to meet the challenges of a rapidly changing world.

Speaking at a packed session in the Swiss Alpine resort town, Annan argued that global institutions—chief among them the United Nations Security Council—remain frozen in a mid-20th century configuration of power that no longer reflects economic and geopolitical realities.

"We are trying to solve 21st century problems with 20th century tools," Annan told the gathering. "The architecture of global governance was designed for a different era, and if we do not modernize it, we risk irrelevance at precisely the moment the world needs coordinated action most."

## A Familiar Refrain, Renewed Urgency

Annan, who led the UN from 1997 to 2006 and has remained an influential voice on international affairs since leaving office, has long advocated for expanding the Security Council to include permanent representation from Africa, Latin America, and a broader swath of Asia. On Thursday, he revisited those themes but framed them within the context of newer crises—climate change, cyberwarfare, mass migration, and widening inequality—that he said demand faster, more legitimate multilateral responses than the current system can deliver.

"When the Council cannot act because of the veto, people suffer and die," he said, an apparent reference to gridlock over conflicts including Syria. "Reform is not a bureaucratic exercise. It is a matter of life and death for millions of people."

He also renewed calls for reforming international financial institutions, arguing that bodies like the International Monetary Fund and World Bank still underrepresent emerging economies despite their growing share of global GDP.

## Business Leaders and Officials React

The remarks drew a mix of applause and pointed questions from the Davos crowd, which included finance ministers, central bank governors, and chief executives of multinational corporations. Several attendees pressed Annan on the practical obstacles to reform, noting that any changes to the Security Council's permanent membership would require approval from the five existing permanent members—the United States, United Kingdom, France, Russia, and China—each of which holds veto power over such changes.

Annan acknowledged the difficulty but pushed back against fatalism. "Every institution that has ever reformed itself was told beforehand that it was impossible," he said. "We cannot let the difficulty of the task excuse us from attempting it."

Business leaders in attendance largely welcomed his emphasis on institutional credibility, with several executives noting that global companies increasingly operate in a policy vacuum on issues like climate regulation and digital governance that outpaces what national governments or international bodies can currently address alone.

## Part of a Broader Davos Conversation

Annan's remarks came amid a broader thread running through this year's forum: growing anxiety among global elites about a perceived erosion of multilateral cooperation, rising nationalism, and strained trust in international institutions. Panels throughout the week have grappled with trade tensions, technological disruption, and what many participants describe as a "crisis of globalization."

Annan, who now chairs the Kofi Annan Foundation and has remained active in peace mediation efforts across Africa and the Middle East, closed his remarks with a call to action directed at the younger generation of leaders in the audience.

"The next generation cannot simply inherit the institutions we built," he said. "They must be willing to rebuild them."

The World Economic Forum continues through the end of the week, with sessions on global trade, climate finance, and technology governance still to come.

# Davos Special Report: World Leaders Confront Economic Recession, Push for Governance Reform

**DAVOS, Switzerland** — As the World Economic Forum convened amid mounting concerns over a deepening global economic slowdown, world leaders, central bankers, and policy experts used the annual gathering to issue urgent calls for reforming international governance institutions they say are ill-equipped to manage today's interconnected crises.

## Recession Fears Dominate Opening Sessions

Opening remarks at this year's forum were markedly somber, with several heads of state acknowledging that synchronized slowdowns across major economies have created what one European finance minister called "a stress test for the entire post-war economic order." Discussions focused heavily on slowing growth, persistent inflationary pressures, supply chain fragility, and rising public debt levels across both developed and emerging markets.

"We are witnessing not just a cyclical downturn, but a structural crisis of coordination," remarked one G20 finance official during a panel session. "Our institutions were built for a different era."

## Calls to Overhaul the IMF and World Bank

A recurring theme throughout the sessions was dissatisfaction with the current architecture of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank. Several emerging market leaders argued that voting structures within these institutions no longer reflect contemporary economic realities, with developing economies—despite representing a growing share of global GDP—remaining underrepresented in decision-making.

"If these institutions are to remain relevant, they must evolve," said a finance minister from a major emerging economy. "Crisis response cannot be dictated by an outdated distribution of power."

Proposals floated included expanded emergency lending capacity, faster disbursement mechanisms for developing nations facing debt distress, and governance reforms to increase the voting share of underrepresented regions.

## WTO Reform and Trade Fragmentation

Trade tensions and the erosion of multilateral trade rules also featured prominently. Business leaders and trade ministers warned that the World Trade Organization's dispute resolution mechanisms have been weakened, contributing to a rise in unilateral tariffs and protectionist measures that many argue are exacerbating the recession's effects.

Calls were made for a "reinvigorated" WTO capable of enforcing rules among major economies and mediating disputes more effectively, alongside renewed dialogue on supply chain resilience and diversification.

## A Divided Response

Not all attendees were aligned on the path forward. Representatives from some advanced economies cautioned against hasty structural changes, arguing that existing institutions, while imperfect, provide stability during turbulent periods. Others emphasized that reform efforts risk becoming mired in geopolitical rivalry, particularly amid ongoing tensions between major powers.

## Looking Ahead

Despite disagreements over specifics, there was broad consensus that the current moment demands serious reflection on global economic governance. Forum organizers indicated that follow-up discussions would continue at upcoming G20 and IMF spring meetings, where concrete reform proposals are expected to be tabled.

As one panel moderator summarized in closing remarks: "Davos this year wasn't about optimism—it was about survival, adaptation, and the uncomfortable recognition that the old rules may no longer serve a new world."

---

*This report reflects proceedings and statements made during World Economic Forum sessions. Further developments will be covered as international discussions on economic governance reform continue.*

**DAVOS** — Business and political leaders serving as co-chairs of this year's World Economic Forum outlined a sobering assessment of interconnected global challenges, warning that financial instability, energy security concerns, and climate change can no longer be addressed in isolation.

## Financial System Under Strain

Several co-chairs emphasized that lingering fragilities in the global financial system continue to threaten economic recovery efforts worldwide. Speakers pointed to elevated debt levels, tightening credit conditions, and uneven growth patterns across regions as evidence that the post-crisis financial architecture remains vulnerable to shocks.

"We cannot afford complacency," one co-chair noted during opening remarks, stressing that regulatory reforms implemented in previous years require continued vigilance and international coordination to prevent future systemic breakdowns.

## Energy Security Concerns Intensify

On energy matters, co-chairs highlighted growing anxiety among both developed and emerging economies about reliable access to affordable energy sources. Geopolitical tensions in key producing regions, coupled with volatile commodity prices, were cited as factors complicating long-term energy planning for governments and businesses alike.

Panelists called for diversified energy portfolios and increased investment in infrastructure that could buffer economies against sudden supply disruptions, framing energy resilience as both an economic and national security imperative.

## Climate Change as Economic Imperative

Perhaps most notably, co-chairs framed climate change not merely as an environmental issue but as a central economic risk factor demanding immediate attention from the private sector. Discussions centered on the need for businesses to integrate climate considerations into core strategic planning rather than treating sustainability as a peripheral concern.

Speakers urged accelerated investment in clean technology and renewable energy infrastructure, arguing that the transition away from carbon-intensive systems represents both an obligation and a significant economic opportunity for forward-thinking enterprises.

## A Call for Integrated Solutions

Throughout the proceedings, a consistent theme emerged: these three challenges—financial stability, energy security, and climate change—are deeply intertwined rather than separate policy silos. Co-chairs repeatedly emphasized that solutions addressing one crisis in isolation risk exacerbating the others.

The overarching message from this year's forum leadership centered on collaborative action, with co-chairs calling on governments, businesses, and civil society to pursue coordinated strategies rather than fragmented responses to what they characterized as fundamentally interconnected global risks.

# World Economic Forum Co-Chairs Call for Overhaul of Global Governance Amid Recession

**Davos, Switzerland (CNN)** -- World leaders and business executives gathered at the World Economic Forum this week delivered a sobering assessment of international institutions, with several co-chairs declaring that existing global governance structures are inadequate to address the ongoing economic crisis.

Former U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told delegates that the financial crisis has exposed fundamental weaknesses in how the world manages shared challenges.

"We have global problems, but we do not have the global institutions or the sense of global solidarity to tackle them," Annan said. "The institutions we built after World War II are simply not designed for the world we live in today."

Annan specifically pointed to the need for reformed international financial oversight, arguing that regulatory bodies had failed to anticipate systemic risks.

"This crisis has taught us that national regulation alone cannot manage what are now deeply interconnected global markets," he said. "We need coordination mechanisms that actually match the scale of the problem."

Media mogul Rupert Murdoch, serving as a forum co-chair, offered a blunter critique, suggesting that both governments and private institutions bore responsibility for the current turmoil.

"Let's be honest -- the system is broken," Murdoch said during a panel discussion. "Whether you're talking about banking regulation, corporate governance, or international cooperation, what we had wasn't working, and pretending otherwise would be a mistake."

Murdoch also weighed in on the media's role in the crisis, acknowledging criticism that news organizations had been slow to flag warning signs.

"We in the media have to ask hard questions about whether we did our job in scrutinizing these institutions before things collapsed," he said.

Other co-chairs echoed calls for structural reform. Several business leaders emphasized that any solution would require unprecedented cooperation between governments, private industry, and international bodies -- a level of coordination many admitted has been historically difficult to achieve.

One recurring theme throughout the discussions was skepticism that current multilateral institutions, including the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, retain the credibility or tools necessary to manage a crisis of this magnitude without significant reform.

Annan, for his part, urged attendees not to let the crisis go to waste.

"This is a moment of opportunity as much as it is a moment of crisis," he said. "If we rebuild the same broken system, we will have failed everyone who is suffering because of this recession."

The forum's discussions are expected to continue as delegates debate specific proposals for regulatory reform, though concrete commitments remained elusive as the conference progressed.
